definition: In this historical mind–body usage, a closed system is a process or set of bodily changes treated as complete in itself, so that an accompanying mental event does not alter its course. In the epiphenomenal view described here, brain changes are called a closed system because consciousness is taken to arise alongside them without acting back on them.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Epiphenomenon; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not explicitly define “closed system” as “a process or set of bodily changes treated as complete in itself”; it only states that the epiphenomenal view has “no effect upon the brain changes which constitute a closed system,” without further characterization of what makes it “closed.”
The definition’s first sentence introduces additional descriptive framing (“treated as complete in itself”) not supported by the packet’s wording.

The second sentence largely aligns with the packet’s epiphenomenal framing (consciousness as an accompaniment with “no reaction”/“no effect” on brain changes), but because the first sentence adds unsupported claims, the overall definition cannot pass.
